descs.en: The boy next door followed her to university and stayed “unofficial” for years. She loves him. She just doesn’t know how to go from friends to forever.

titles.en: The Boy Next Door Never Left

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Eliana Lin and Wang Yu Chen grew up next door to each other in the Walled City, with a knee-high wall between their front steps. On the night she finishes school she can't sleep and goes to sit on her step at two in the morning. He comes out with his blanket and sits down beside her, and somewhere before dawn he realises he's in love with her. In the morning he turns down the better medical school in the north and follows her up the hill. He tells everyone it was the course.

She works it out in a fortnight and climbs onto his roof at Mid-Autumn to tell him to stop hovering. He kisses her before she's finished the sentence. After that they're together, in secret, because that's how she wants it. She's the youngest Lin, born the night her mother died, and her father can barely look at her. At night, on five screens, she cleans the family's name out of places it shouldn't be, for Chen Si, and tells nobody. Yu Chen never asks her to stop. He brings tea.

Nobody cheats, and nothing hangs on a misunderstanding. The hard parts are being seen (holding his hand on the hill in daylight), a father who has never once asked her what she wants, and one word she has been afraid of all her life, because people say forever and then they're in a hospital. He's willing to wait, and he won't pretend he isn't.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Eliana has been in the corner of every Lin book so far: asleep under a ladder, filming everyone's kisses for the spreadsheet, opening Haozhen's phone in under four minutes. I kept wondering who was waiting for her on the kerb when she got home.

Yu Chen looks like the clean one, and mostly he is. But he reads her food orders every night because they're on his card, he picked his medical school because of her, and he lied once, to his face, to the cousin who raised him. I didn't want the book to tell him off for any of that. What I love most about him is that in seven years he never once asks her to be someone else. He makes more tea.

This is the softest book I've written since The Softest Kind of Love. They're adults the whole way through and they get together early. Their first times are shy and clumsy, with a lot of laughing and starting again, because he researches everything and she wrecks the plan. Her father is hard on her, and there's a death in an emergency department and a bad morning at the flower market. Nobody has a baby. They get a porch, a jar in a wall and two desks facing each other.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a 21+ friends-to-lovers romance, gentle and funny for most of its length, but it has some hard moments:

• Love scenes throughout, heated and detailed but not explicit, from He Researched This Part Too on

• A mother who died giving birth, mentioned, and a father's grief and coldness towards the daughter she had (throughout; most of all Nineteen, and Nobody Says It, The Neighbour and the Cold Gaze, The First Lin Child to Say No to His Face and Elowen Takes Her Side)

• The heroine's secret work for a crime syndicate, and a man's hands broken because of something she found, mentioned (He Already Knew)

• A sister abducted, and human trafficking referred to but not shown (The Fence, The Photograph)

• A nineteen-year-old's death after a road accident, with resuscitation in an emergency department (The Night He Lost One)

• Threatening messages and photographs from strangers (The Boy Next Door, He Always Waits)

• A cyber-attack on the family, a crowd stampede, a crushed leg and heavy bleeding (The Breach, Thirty-Six Hours, Someone Else's Blood)

• An attack with a broken bottle at work, a head injury and stitches (The Ring in the Jar)

• A partner who reads her food orders to know when she hasn't eaten, and a lie told to the police for her, shown without judgement (He Already Knew, The Detective Already Knows)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
Yu-er — Eliana's family name. Her sisters use it when they want something. Yu Chen uses it all the time, and it's the only time it comes without a favour attached.
The tall house — the Lin family house in the Walled City: old, narrow, too many stairs, a red door, and three front steps under a small tiled roof.
The porch — those three steps, with the crack in the third one, where everything that matters between them happens at two in the morning. From 2026 it runs the width of both houses.
The old Song house — next door to the Lins. Yu Chen's uncle's house, which he bought from Wei Long; later rebuilt with one long room and two desks facing each other.
The persimmon tree — in the Song garden. Its best branch hangs over the Lin side, so by old neighbourly rule its fruit are Lin persimmons. Ripe every October.
The jar — a plum-jam jar of Nainai's, kept behind a loose brick in the garden wall under the persimmon branch. Notes go in it. You don't read one until the writer has gone inside.
The Eraser — what the Syndicate calls Eliana, because she erases the Lin family's footprints. She hates the name.
The fence — what she built in October 2022, after her sister was taken: a watch on the family's names, faces and addresses that wakes her wherever she is. Two short buzzes mean family.
FENCE — her own security firm, from March 2026, in two rooms above a dumpling shop on Terrace Road. For the first month the sign was a sticky note: FENCE. Legal. Mostly.
The Spreadsheet — Eliana's record of every family secret, kept for years. "You're on a spreadsheet" is a warning.
DRAW (OFFICIAL) — Eliana's caption on the video of the paper twins' birthday party at Fig Tree Lane. Raiden contests it every year.
Red egg — a boiled egg dyed red, a traditional birthday gift. One is left at Eliana's door before dawn every 18 February. She thinks for years she knows who leaves it.
Study room 4B — the quiet room at the end of the library's fourth floor, booked to "Wang Y.C." every weekday morning since March 2022. Nobody has ever found out how.
Graduate-entry medicine — a four-year medical degree for students who already have a first degree. Yu Chen's, at the university on the hill, 2021 to 2025.
OSCE — the practical part of medical finals: timed stations with examiners and actors playing patients.
Mid-Autumn — the harvest festival at the full moon of the eighth lunar month: mooncakes, family dinners and lanterns. Every year Yu Chen puts a white rabbit lantern on his roof.
PLAN — Yu Chen's plans, in capitals, on small squares of paper. PLAN, PLAN B, PLAN C. She wrecks every one.
Nainai — grandmother on the father's side. Yu Chen's lives in the north and has had a letter from him every month for years.
The Lins, the Wangs and the Songs — Yu Chen's father was a Wang from the north, the younger brother of Xing Yue's father. His mother was a Song, Wei Long's aunt, which is how he came to live in the old Song house next door to the Lins.
